blocks.p: The second aftertaste from the widow's door would not leave him alone. Rei went back to Adachi the next morning and stood at her threshold until he had it again, faint and cold. Then he followed it.

It was slow work. A trail like that does not run along roads. It ran along the places where the veil had been scraped, and those places were scattered. He rode a few stops, got off, walked until the taste grew weak, then turned and found it again a street away. By noon he had crossed three wards. He drank barley tea from a vending machine on a station platform and pressed the cold can to his neck. On one train a mother sat with two small boys in matching caps, all three of them asleep against each other, their heads rolling together at every curve. On a footbridge an old man in a straw hat had stopped to look down at the tracks, holding a shopping bag full of fruit. Ordinary people, going home for Obon. None of them could feel the thing Rei was following through their streets.

And slowly, the trail taught him something the Healer's threads never could. There was another worker in this city. Gin's mercy closed wounds and tied the grateful into one careful tally. This other thing did not close anything. It tore.

blocks.break: The underpass by the freight line

blocks.cap: The long pedestrian underpass beneath the freight line

blocks.p: The trail ended at a long pedestrian underpass beneath a station, where the freight line crossed overhead. Every few minutes a long goods train rumbled above, and the whole tunnel hummed with it. The low end flooded whenever it rained, and the tiles there were stained up to the height of a child. Rei knew this place from Gin's pages. He had read them so often that he could recite them.

doc.title: Gin's archive. Disturbed Areas. The Station Underpass
lines: Walked the freight underpass again. Still wrong on the 11th. Did not stay. G.U.
THIN SPOT. A migrating thin spot. Worst in the cold.
A place where the membrane has worn through... and the wear migrates with the district's mood.
A Grid handler keeps a dog at the south mouth most nights. The CVD flags it. The Grid actually watches it.
Everything is more visible to everyone here... and entities see you regardless of rank. Carry less stability in than you think you need.
I have crossed easiest, and been noticed worst, in that underpass. The two turn out to be the same fact wearing different coats.

blocks.p: The dog was there at the south mouth. It was a heavy brown animal lying on a folded blanket with its chin on its paws. It lifted its head when Rei came down the steps and watched him without moving. It did not follow him in. Rei understood that as the warning it was.

It was August, not winter, so the underpass should have been at its quietest. It was not quiet. The veil here was not being soothed. It was being worn down on purpose, scraped thinner and thinner, the way a person files a lock until the bolt gives way. Gin's seams felt tight and tidy, like a bandage pulled hard. These felt like the second before a window breaks. Rei's gift pulled back so hard that he tasted copper in his mouth.

Under the scraping there was something older, and he recognised it from Gin's book too. It was heavy, and it was not thinking. The 2011 dead had never been properly seen home, and their grief had gathered in the low places of the city the way rainwater gathers. Gin had written about exactly this.

doc.title: CVD Entity Classification Reference. Chapter 11. Suffering Beings
lines: A suffering being is not an entity in the conventional sense. It is the residue of an intelligence... the emotional material that remained after the self dissolved at crossing, concentrated in the location where the dissolution occurred.
It is not thinking. It is not choosing. It is not directing its effects at anyone. It simply weighs what it weighs, and if you are in the space, you feel the weight.
The person is gone. Demons retain intelligence. Spirits retain personality. Suffering beings have no continuity with the person they came from.

It cannot be reasoned with, communicated with, redirected, or resolved through relationship. It can only be cleared, or managed. This is not exorcism. There is nothing to remove. There is something to process.

Margin, G.U. A suffering being is grief that found no floor to land on. After 2011 there was a great deal of grief and nowhere near enough floor. Be gentle when you meet one. It was a person's love before it was your problem.

blocks.p: That was what the boy in Gin's ledger had been hearing in the gutters when it rained. Not voices. Weight. And now someone was using that weight like sandpaper against the wall.

blocks.break: A back room the Grid kept that month

blocks.cap: A back room the Grid kept that month

blocks.p: The Grid had a name for the one doing it. Rei got it that evening, in a back room above a shuttered shop. The Grid was using the room that month and would not be using it the next. He was there on a vouch. One of Gin's people, someone who owed his brother the dangerous kind of debt, had vouched for him to a man, and the man had sent him here.

He had walked the last part. The street was narrow and dark, lined with closed shutters and small bars that had not opened yet. A ramen shop by the tracks was the only bright window, and a cook stood outside it smoking in a white cap, watching the trains go by. Rei found the door the man had described, between a shuttered shop and a stairwell, and went up.

Nobody in the room was in charge. People came up the stairs, put something down or picked something up, and left again. An electric fan turned its head from side to side and moved the hot air around without cooling it. A courier sat on an upturned crate with a kit bag on her knees. The bag had come, she said, through three pairs of hands before hers. It would go through one more before it reached the person who needed it.
She gave Rei the name over her shoulder while she checked the bag's straps. She spoke in the hushed way people use for things they hope are exaggerated.

"They call it the Inverted God," she said. "Or its aspirant does. It isn't a god yet. Its mouth is a boy called Kaito. He was a medium before he was a vessel, and now there's not much left of him but the mouth." She pulled a strap tight. "The thing itself doesn't come to the pools. It sits somewhere else, in somebody else, and talks through him."

Rei understood the words. A medium is a person the dead can speak through, for a little while, by permission. A vessel is a body that something else has moved into and kept. Kaito had been the first. Now he was the second.
"What does it want?"

"It says the veil is a muzzle the living strapped onto the dead. It says tearing it isn't a catastrophe, it's emancipation." She looked at him properly then. "The old people say there's something at the centre that holds the wall shut. This one wants to be the opposite of that. It wants to tear the wall open and rule whatever pours through. It doesn't want a seat at the table. It wants to turn the table over and salt the ground where it stood."
By every measure the factions had, she said, it was the bigger horror in this city by far. Then she put the bag on her shoulder and went down the stairs, and someone else came up.

That was exactly the problem. Rei felt it close around him in that hot back room. The moment there was a bigger monster, every faction with a grade and a grievance would turn toward it. And the quiet, reasonable, mercy-making thing wearing his brother would start to look, by comparison, like the lesser evil. The manageable one. The one a sensible person might even join forces with against the worse one. The Healer had not summoned the Inverted God. But in all its long patient life it had never been given a better gift than a rival so monstrous that it made the Healer look like a saviour.

blocks.cap: Kaito, the courier who preaches in the drained pool

blocks.p: Kaito preached in a drained public swimming pool in the dead hour after midnight. Rei walked there through streets that had gone quiet at last. The Obon lanterns were still lit on some houses, and a konbini on the corner glowed like an aquarium, a single clerk inside reading a magazine. The pool had been closed since the summer before. A chain hung loose on the gate. The blue paint on its walls had cracked into shapes like the maps of countries that did not exist.
About forty people stood on the tiled floor of the deep end. They all had the widow's look. Accounted for. Grateful. Leashed. But their leashes ran the other way, toward tearing instead of binding.

Kaito was younger than the fear around him had suggested. He could not have been more than twenty. He stood in the shallow end with his hands loose at his sides. His eyes did not quite follow the people he looked at, as if someone else were doing the looking through them. He did not rant. He grieved, out loud, so precisely that the cicadas outside sounded like applause.

"They drowned in front of us," he said of 2011. "And we built a wall so we would not have to keep hearing them, and we called the wall mercy." He let the words go out over the old painted lane lines. "Since 2009 the wall here in Kita has been failing. Since 2011 it has been failing faster. They tell you that is the danger. I tell you it is the dead, knocking. I am only proposing we stop lying about what the wall is."
Forty heads nodded. Rei's own head wanted to nod too, and he hated it for that.

There it was again. A true thing, set at a slight, deadly angle. Kaito was right that the veil was partly a wall the living had built so that they would not hear the dead. He was wrong, terribly and completely wrong, about what happens to a city when that wall comes down. Rei stood at the edge of the empty pool, with the ghost of chlorine still in the air. He understood that he was now holding two arguments, and each held enough truth to drown a person in. His brother's captor was the more patient of the two, and the more polite. And everyone with the power to act was going to mistake politeness for safety.
Kaito found him on the way out. These things always seemed to. He fell into step beside Rei on the cracked path to the gate. He knew Rei's name, which meant the seams had been talking.

"Your brother and I want opposite things," he said, almost kindly. His voice was a young man's voice, but the words had an older weight in them, as if they had been chosen somewhere far away and only delivered here. "That should comfort you. It won't. You've already worked out that opposite things can want the same Tuesday."
He let that sit. Then he stopped at the gate and said, "When the seat comes vacant, ask yourself who benefits from the wall being thin. It isn't only me."

Rei walked home under the lanterns with that sentence sitting in his chest. A taxi went by with its light on, slow, hoping. Two drunk office workers sang a few lines of an old song outside a closed bar and then forgot the rest. At the flat he did not sleep. He took Gin's archive down again and turned to the chapter on the Grid. He had been moving inside it for a week on a stranger's word, and he still did not understand what he had walked into. Gin would have written it down.
